sections.b: 1 Peter writes to believers, probably mostly Gentile, across five regions of Asia Minor who had become outsiders in their own towns. It tells them who they are (born again, chosen, God's house and royal priesthood), how to live under pressure (do good, submit where possible, return blessing for abuse, give a gentle defense of their hope) and why to hope (Christ suffered, was made alive and rules over every power). It ends with greetings from 'Babylon', most likely Rome.

common: Most readers take 'Babylon' in 5:13 as Rome.
uncommon: Erasmus and Calvin took 'Babylon' to be the city in Mesopotamia.

sections.h: Peter's letter and Peter in Rome
sections.b: 1 Peter presents the apostle as 'a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ' (5:1), writing through Silvanus with Mark beside him from 'Babylon' (5:12-13). Eusebius reports from Papias and Clement of Alexandria that Peter wrote it 'in Rome itself' and called the city 'by a figure, Babylon'. 1 Clement 5 and Ignatius' To the Romans 4 are the earliest outside texts that connect Peter with Rome and his martyrdom. Whether Peter wrote the letter himself is debated (see the topic 1 Peter).

1 Peter 3:19 says Christ, made alive in the spirit, 'went and made a proclamation to the spirits in prison' who disobeyed in Noah's day, and 4:6 that 'the good news was announced even to the dead'. Readers have seen here the fallen angels of Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch, imprisoned until judgment, to whom the risen Christ proclaimed his victory; the dead, to whom he went between his death and resurrection (Catholic and Orthodox teaching); or the people of Noah's day, to whom Christ preached through Noah (Augustine). The verse is the main biblical text for the creed's 'he descended into hell'.

common: Many Catholic and Orthodox Christians read 3:19 as Christ's descent to free the righteous dead.
uncommon: The Latter-day Saints read 3:19 and 4:6 together as the basis of preaching the gospel to the dead in the spirit world (Doctrine and Covenants 138).

sections.b: 1 Peter calls the whole church 'a holy priesthood that brings spiritual sacrifices' and 'a royal priesthood', taking the words of Exodus 19:6 in their Greek form. The noun is collective: the community, not each person alone, is the priesthood. The verse became the main text for the Reformation's priesthood of all believers and for Catholic and Orthodox teaching on the common priesthood of the baptized; the churches differ on how it relates to ordained ministers.

1 Peter says the water of Noah's flood has its counterpart in baptism, which 'saves you now as well', not as a bath but as 'the pledge of a good conscience made to God', 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ'. The verse is one of the New Testament's plainest statements that baptism saves, and the churches read its qualifications differently.

sections.h: 'Babylon' as the place of writing (1 Peter 5:13)
sections.b: 1 Peter sends greetings from 'her who is in Babylon, chosen along with you'. Since ancient times most readers have taken Babylon as a name for Rome, as in Revelation 14:8 and 17-18; Eusebius reports this from Papias and Clement of Alexandria. Erasmus and Calvin argued for the Mesopotamian city, and some have proposed the Roman fortress called Babylon in Egypt.

If 'Babylon' in 1 Peter 5:13 is Rome, the letter is a word from the church at the empire's center, with Peter, Silvanus and Mark, to scattered churches in the provinces, and it treats the capital as a place of exile, as Revelation does.

sections.h: Resident aliens and temporary residents (1 Peter)
sections.b: 1 Peter calls its readers parepidemoi, 'temporary residents' (1:1; 2:11), and paroikoi, 'resident aliens' (2:11), and their life a paroikia (1:17), the words Abraham uses of himself in the Greek of Genesis 23:4. Scholars debate whether this describes the readers' social and legal standing, as John H. Elliott argued, or their life as believers whose home is with God.
sections.refs: 1 Peter 1:1; 1 Peter 1:17; 1 Peter 2:11; Genesis 23:4; Psalm 39:12; Hebrews 11:13; Ephesians 2:19

sections.b: 1 Peter opens with 'the Dispersion' (1:1), the word for Jewish communities outside the land (Eusebius and Calvin took the readers to be Jewish believers; many modern readers think the churches were mostly Gentile), and closes with greetings from 'Babylon' (5:13). The letter reads its readers' life as a kind of exile, and quotes Isaiah 40's comfort to the exiles (1:24-25).
sections.refs: 1 Peter 1:1; 1 Peter 1:24-25; 1 Peter 5:13; Isaiah 40:6-8; John 7:35; James 1:1

sections.h: Born again through the resurrection and the word (1 Peter)
sections.b: 1 Peter uses the verb anagennao, 'give new birth', twice: God gave believers new birth 'through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead' (1:3), and 'from seed that cannot decay: God's word' (1:23). The newborn then crave 'the milk of the word' (2:2).
sections.refs: 1 Peter 1:3; 1 Peter 1:23; 1 Peter 2:2; John 3:3-5; Titus 3:5; James 1:18

sections.b: 1 Peter strings together Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14 and adds that believers are 'stones that live', built on Christ into a spiritual house. Romans 9:33 joins two of the same texts.
sections.refs: 1 Peter 2:4-8; Isaiah 28:16; Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 8:14; Romans 9:33; Ephesians 2:20

sections.b: 1 Peter gives a church that was probably mostly Gentile the titles of Israel from Exodus 19:6, Isaiah 43:20-21 and Hosea (2:9-10), calls it 'the Dispersion' (1:1), and calls unbelieving outsiders 'the Gentiles' (2:12), while never mentioning Israel or the Jews. Readers differ on whether this means replacement, inclusion, or borrowed language.

1 Peter's code begins with the emperor and governors, speaks to household slaves but not to masters, and gives wives, many with unbelieving husbands, six verses, against one for husbands. Each instruction is grounded in Christ's example or in God's judgment. Its purpose is debated: to reduce hostility by showing good order, or to give a marginal group its own identity.

1 Peter tells household slaves to submit 'not only for the good and fair ones, but for the crooked ones too', grounding this in Christ's unjust suffering, and it calls the suffering unjust. Sermons to slaves by Bishop William Meade of Virginia, quoted by Harriet Beecher Stowe in A Key to Uncle Tom's Cabin (1853), told slaves that when punished, 'whether you really deserve it or not', they must 'bear it patiently', language close to 2:19-20; Stowe called such discourses 'hard-hearted and unfeeling to the last degree'.

1 Peter tells wives to submit to their husbands, mainly with unbelieving husbands in view, and calls Sarah's 'lord' a model (Genesis 18:12); husbands are to honor their wives as 'co-heirs ... of the grace of life'. The site's card at Ephesians 5 sets out the churches' views on headship.

1 Peter weaves Isaiah 53 into its picture of Christ's suffering: no trickery in his mouth (53:9), bearing sins (53:12), healed by his welts (53:5), sheep gone astray (53:6). The passage was written first for household slaves who suffered unjustly.

1 Peter's readers suffer slander and abuse for their faith; the letter calls this a test of faith like fire on gold (1:7), a share in Christ's sufferings (4:13), and a calling that follows Christ's model (2:21), and it warns them not to suffer for real wrongdoing (4:15).

Many scholars read 'the spirits in prison, who had refused to obey once, long ago ... in the days of Noah' as the angels who sinned before the flood, held in a prison as in 1 Enoch ('This place is the prison of the angels', 1 Enoch 21:10). 2 Peter 2:4-5 and Jude 1:6 speak of the same angels.
1 Peter counts the saved in the ark, 'eight souls', and says the water that carried them safe has its counterpart in baptism. The few saved in Noah's day encourage a small minority.

sections.h: The flood as a picture of baptism (1 Peter 3:20-21)
sections.b: 1 Peter reads the flood water, which drowned the world and carried the ark, as the pattern whose counterpart is baptism.

1 Peter 3:21 calls baptism the antitypon, 'counterpart', of the flood, one of the sources of the word 'antitype' in Christian typology. Hebrews 9:24, the word's only other New Testament use, has it for the earthly sanctuary as a copy of the heavenly one.

1 Peter calls the writer 'your fellow elder' and tells the elders to shepherd God's flock, 'overseeing it', not for money and not acting as lords, but as patterns for the flock, under Christ the Chief Shepherd. Elders and overseeing go together here, as in Acts 20:17, 28 and Titus 1:5-7.
sections.refs: 1 Peter 5:1-5; 1 Peter 2:25; Acts 20:17; Acts 20:28; Titus 1:5-7; John 21:15-17

sections.b: 1 Peter calls Christ 'the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls' (2:25) and 'the Chief Shepherd' (5:4), and tells the elders to shepherd God's flock (5:2), the charge Jesus gave Peter in John 21:16.
1 Peter calls the devil 'your opponent', the word for an adversary in court, prowling 'like a lion that roars', and tells believers to stand up against him, as James 4:7 does.

1 Peter says 'Through Silvanus, a brother I count faithful, I have written you these few lines' (5:12). 'Through' can name the secretary or drafter who gave the letter its Greek form (the 'secretarial hypothesis') or the courier who carried it (John H. Elliott's view). Both readings are open.
1 Peter sends greetings from 'Mark, my son'. Eusebius reports Papias' and Clement's account that Mark wrote down Peter's preaching in Rome and that Peter mentions Mark in his first letter.

sections.h: Honor the king, fear God (1 Peter 2:13-17)
sections.b: 1 Peter tells believers to submit to the emperor and governors 'because of the Lord', and sums up: 'Give honor to all people. Love the brothers. Fear God. Give honor to the king.' Only God is feared; the emperor is honored as all people are.

1 Peter calls the emperor 'the king', the usual Greek title in the East, and gives him honor but not fear, which is kept for God (2:17). Pliny's letter from Bithynia-Pontus (about AD 112) shows former Christians proving their loyalty by offering incense and wine to the emperor's image and cursing Christ.

sections.h: 'The end of all things has come close' (1 Peter 4:7)
sections.b: 1 Peter places its readers 'in the last of the times' (1:20) and says 'the end of all things has come close' (4:7), drawing practical conclusions: prayer, love, hospitality and service.

sections.h: Gifts for speaking and serving (1 Peter 4:10-11)
sections.b: 1 Peter says 'each of you has been given a gift' and divides the gifts into speaking and serving, each used as stewards of 'God's many-sided grace'.
1 Peter tells believers to open their homes to one another as guests 'without grumbling', a need in churches whose messengers and teachers traveled between towns.

sections.h: 'You will be holy, because I am holy' (1 Peter 1:15-16)
sections.b: 1 Peter quotes Leviticus' call to holiness for its readers, without the food laws, as a call to a different way of life among the nations.

sections.h: Ransom, the lamb and the tree (1 Peter)
sections.b: 1 Peter speaks of being ransomed 'with blood of great worth, like that of a lamb with no flaw and no stain' (1:18-19), of Christ carrying 'our sins up in his body onto the tree' (2:24) and of his suffering 'for sins, a single time, the one who was righteous for those who were not' (3:18).

1 Peter calls believers 'chosen' in keeping with God's foreknowledge (1:1-2), 'a chosen family' (2:9), and says those who stumble over the word were 'set' for it (2:8). Readers differ over what foreknowledge and appointment mean.
The writer calls himself 'a witness of the sufferings of Christ'. 1 Clement 5 says Peter 'suffered martyrdom', and Eusebius reports that he was crucified in Rome.

sections.h: God gives grace to the humble (1 Peter 5:5-6)
sections.b: 1 Peter quotes the Greek of Proverbs 3:34, 'God takes his stand against the proud, but to the humble he gives grace', as James 4:6 does, and tells all believers to 'tie humility on toward one another'.

1 Peter calls for a love of the brothers 'that does not pretend' (1:22), a love 'that never slackens' because 'love lays a cover over a great number of sins' (4:8, from Proverbs 10:12), and ends with 'a kiss of love' (5:14).
sections.refs: 1 Peter 1:22; 1 Peter 3:8; 1 Peter 4:8; 1 Peter 5:14; Proverbs 10:12; James 5:20
